newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE-Peru rebels go Japanese during hostage siege.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Peru rebels go Japanese during hostage siege.

text.p: As one of Peru's most feared rebel leaders, Nestor Cerpa was called "Commandante." Now he is getting used to being called "Cerpa-san" -- Japanese for "Mister Cerpa."

Since taking up temporary residence at Ambassador Morihisa Aoki's residence in Lima, he has also hung up his boots, a trademark of any respected jungle combatant, and sports sandals or bare feet indoors, Japanese style.

More than three months after arriving uninvited at Aoki's cocktail party -- actually he blasted his way in along with 20-odd other Marxist rebels -- Cerpa and his fighters are catching on fast to some of their unwilling host's habits, Red Cross members and doctors who regularly enter the residence say. These include exercising to the beat of Japanese music, eating sushi and even taking language lessons from some of their 72 hostages, two dozen of whom are Japanese.

"In the beginning we were just bringing in a few rations of Japanese food, but now almost everyone is eating it," said a doctor accompanying Red Cross members who take food and drinks to the compound every day. "The hostages realised that it is also more healthy, given the sedentary lifestyle they are leading."

Of the 500-odd dignitaries taken hostage when the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) broke into Aoki's cocktail party on Dec. 17, only 72 men remain captive. They include the ambassadors of Bolivia and Japan, Peru's foreign affairs and agriculture ministers Francisco Tudela and Rodolfo Munante, President Alberto Fujimori's brother Pedro, generals, diplomats and businessmen.

Stretching exercises take place every afternoon, when a local radio station runs its one-hour programme devoted to the hostages. The programme includes a "taisa" -- a tune played at Japanese factories to help workers exercise.

"Hands up, hands down," says the song in Japanese, and the hardened Peruvian rebels, who are more used to training in the jungle than to walking the tiled floors of a diplomatic mansion in an upscale district of the bustling capital, dutifully lift and lower their arms.
"Initially only the Japanese exercised to the beat of the music, but soon all started to join in because they needed it," the doctor said.
Japanese language lessons are also very popular in the residence, with two young women guerrillas among the most dedicated students.
Peruvian intelligence sources recently told the daily La Republica they were surprised at how well the hostages and their captors were getting along.

"We have heard frequent conversations between Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, Ambassador Aoki and leaders Nestor Cerpa and Rolly Rojas," one intelligence official told the newspaper. "They discuss politics but they also talk about personal experiences -- as if they were old pals. We have not heard anyone raising his voice. No screams, no sobs. There's an incredible degree of solidarity."
INCREASED DEMAND FOR SUSHI NO PROBLEM

The increased demand for sushi will hardly pose logistic problems in Lima -- the 80,000-strong Japanese Peruvian community is the second largest in Latin America, behind Brazil's. Its most prominent member, of course, is President Fujimori, who married -- and later divorced -- Susana Higuchi, also a "nikkei," as the Japanese Peruvians call themselves.

The current administration has three nikkei Cabinet ministers including the speaker of Congress, Jaime Yoshiyama. And visitors to Peru sometimes remark that Japanese and native Peruvians, the majority of whom are of Inca Indian descent, often share striking physical similarities.

Nikkei members also say the crisis has drawn the community together and given many members a new sense of self-esteem. And it has intensified already blooming ties between Lima and Tokyo, with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto calling Fujimori on the telephone frequently to discuss the crisis, which is being followed blow-by-blow by many Japanese reporters on the scene.
Since Fujimori came to power in 1990, Japan, one of the world's richest nations, has become a major donor of aid to Peru, about half of whose population lives below the poverty line.

But for all the sushi, taisa and friendly chat, the harsh reality remains unchanged -- the longer the hostage crisis goes on, the greater the danger of a violent outcome, even of one triggered by accident.

When Cerpa and his fighters exercise in the mined and bobby-trapped residence, hand grenades dangle from their belts. And when they pass a cigarette to a hostage while exchanging anecdotes, they do so with one hand, while the other firmly clutches an assault rifle loaded with live ammunition.
